https://telex.hu/kulfold/2026/08/03/oros.text: Menü Kereső Oroszok által ukránnak mondott drón zuhant le egy strandon, heten meghaltak Külföld frissítve Klág Dávid Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Drón csapódott be egy dél-orosz strandon, az esetben hét ember, köztük három gyerek halt meg – írja a BBC orosz források alapján. Az eset a Krasznodari határterület régiójában történt, a Fekete-tenger partján, Gelendzsik üdülővárosban. A terület kormányzója, Venyiamin Kondratyjev szerint összesen negyvenen sérültek meg, tizenheten kórházba kerültek. Ukrajna egyelőre még nem kommentálta az esetet. A BBC cikke szerint nem egyértelmű, hogy mi okozta a becsapódást. Ukrán Telegram-csatornákon az a hír terjed, hogy a drón azért zuhant le, mert oroszok zavarták a jeleit. Orosz források szerint a becsapódás előtt lövések dördültek el, ami azt is jelentheti, hogy megpróbálták orosz katonák lelőni a szerkezetet. A Reuters szerint Kondratyjev is egy korábbi nyilatkozatában arról beszélt, hogy drónalkatrészek zuhantak le a strandon. A helyiek nem hallottak légitámadásra utaló szirénákat. Ukrajna és Oroszország is azt állítja, hogy nem támadnak meg szándékosan civileket a több mint négy éve tartó háborúban. Ukrajna július végén a legnagyobb orosz online kereskedő, a Wildberries raktárait támadta drónokkal Volgográdban, Tatárföldön és Udmurtföldön. Gelendzsik közelében található az a luxuskomplexum, amit Putyin kastélyaként is emlegetnek. Tavaly ott egy lezuhant drón okozott erdőtüzet . https://www.dw.com/en/pakistan-islamabad.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JOEK The fire was believed to have been caused by a malfunctioning air conditioning unit Image: Akhtar Soomro/REUTERS Advertisement A least 14 infants were killed after a fire broke out at the maternity ward of a hospital in Islamabad, Pakistan , on Wednesday. "A fire broke out on the third floor of the MCH Ward at PIMS Hospital," the district office of Islamabad said, referring to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences. The blaze broke out at around 6:45 a.m. (0145 UTC) when an air conditioning unit exploded inside the nursery, rescuers said. Distraught parents gathered outside the hospital Image: Aamir Qureshi/AFP Officials said 16 newborns were in the ward at the time, adding that one was rescued. Outside the hospital, a nurse read out the names of babies who had perished as their families gathered around. "I lost my daughter. She was only three days old," one father told the AFP news agency. "My wife was in the ward. They took everyone out. We were sitting on the road waiting for help." Investigation underway Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has ordered an immediate investigation into the incident. "A tragedy involving children is an irreparable loss," he said in a statement. "Those ​responsible should be identified, and ​the strictest action should be taken." The incident is one of the deadliest hospital fires in recent memory in Pakistan, where healthcare is subsidized but public hospitals are often are under-resourced and overburdened. Ambassadors from the EU’s 27 member states failed to reach agreement at a meeting early on Tuesday – their third session in around 24 hours on the topic. The senior diplomats will reconvene later today just hours ahead of a legal deadline. Without an agreement sanctions on nearly 3,000 people and entities accused of supporting the war on Ukraine will lapse at the end of Tuesday 22 September. The list includes Vladimir Putin, foreign minister Sergei Lavrov, Duma deputies, Russia’s major banks, energy companies and military industrial complex. The EU can also agree a short-term extension pending a longer agreement and has already prolonged the deadline by one week. One diplomat suggested

https://news.antiwar.com/2026/10/06/lith.text: Lithuania Moves To Lift Nuclear Weapons Ban as Trump Considers Permanent US Base Lithuania’s parliament on Tuesday took the first step toward lifting a ban on the deployment of nuclear weapons in its territory, a move that comes after President Trump said he’s considering establishing a permanent US military base in the country. One hundred and six members of Lithuania’s 141-seat unicameral parliament, the Seimas, voted to advance a constitutional amendment that would repeal a ban on weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases in Lithuania. A second vote is needed to advance the amendment, and that will be held on January 12, 2027. At least 94 members of the Seimas must support it for the change to be made. Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda announced in July that he was initiating an amendment to repeal the ban, outlined in Article 137 of the Lithuanian Constitution, and said the idea has “practically unanimous” support in the Seimas. Nauseda and other proponents of repealing the ban say it’s needed for Lithuania to fully participate in NATO’s “nuclear deterrence.” The move will open up Lithuania to potentially host US nuclear weapons under NATO’s nuclear sharing program, under which the US has nukes deployed in Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands, and Turkey. Lithuania’s move comes after Finland, which, like Lithuania, shares a border with Russia, lifted its prohibition on nuclear weapons . Russia strongly condemned both moves and has warned it will respond. “Neither of these developments will contribute to stability and predictability on the European continent,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Tuesday, referring to Lithuania’s parliament voting to repeal both the ban on nuclear weapons and foreign military bases. “On the contrary, they will, to our regret, mark yet another significant escalation of tensions. As for Russia, of course, Moscow will be forced to take all necessary measures to guarantee its own security,” Peskov added. The US has troops deployed in Lithuania on a rotational basis but doesn’t have a permanent base in the country, something Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius has said the country is willing to fund. When asked about the proposal, President Trump said he would consider it. “They’re friends of mine; they’re great people, so we’ll certainly look at it. They are great people,” Trump said. “I know so many people in that country; they’re great people.” If you liked this article, please support Antiwar.com. We are 100% reader-supported. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text: A firefighter and a resident tackle a blaze in Spain’s Zamora province in July 2026. Photograph: Ümit Bektaş/Reuters View image in fullscreen A firefighter and a resident tackle a blaze in Spain’s Zamora province in July 2026. Photograph: Ümit Bektaş/Reuters Spain Spain has been hit hard by the climate crisis. Why are politicians saying so little about it before the election? Wildfires and floods can do little to move climate change up voters’ list of priorities, experts say Sam Jones in Navas del Rey Wed 25 Nov 2026 08.00 EST Last modified on Wed 25 Nov 2026 11.37 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google B eneath the blackened branches of a pine tree that rises high above a landscape of scorched hillsides and the odd charred and ruined house, two older men address the obvious. Four months after one of the summer’s many wildfires threatened to devour the hamlet of El Morro , an hour west of Madrid, local people are still counting the cost and awaiting compensation. “Look at that house,” said Esteban Pérez, pointing to one of the properties that did not make it through July’s flames. “Everything inside is scorched, completely destroyed. You can still see the windows, but they’re gutted. The entire structure of the house next to mine had to be torn down, too. And they’ve given the owner nothing so far.” His friend nods and offers a more laconic observation: “We’re still screwed here.” View image in fullscreen A property destroyed by wildfire in El Morro, a hamlet an hour west of Madrid. Photograph: Sam Jones/The Guardian And yet, for all the abundant recent evidence of the effects of the climate crisis around Spain’s capital and in the eastern region of Valencia, which is still recovering from the deadly floods that killed more than 230 people two years ago , there has been little mention of the issue as the country prepares for this week’s snap general election . Pérez is not surprised that the politicians are keener to focus on housing and immigration than on Spain’s immense vulnerability to climatic disasters and the attendant costs. “The thing is, they only talk about whatever interests them during the campaign,” he said. “If something doesn’t interest them, they don’t talk about it.” Four hundred kilometres to the east in the Valencian municipality of Benetússer, Rut Moyano, a member of the local emergency and reconstruction committee, has been stunned by the lack of focus on the climate crisis. “It’s not just the floods we have experienced, there are also the forest fires; the temperatures the Mediterranean is reaching; the fact that we spend our summers in a state of permanent heatwave, and the droughts,” she said. “Everything is changing because of these factors, but it’s as if there’s an attempt – I don’t know if it’s an intentional silencing – but certainly a failure to give the issue the importance it truly deserves.” Despite the lack of stump speeches and calls to action, climate policies do feature in this year’s manifestos. The ruling socialist party – which describes the climate emergency as “one of the greatest challenges of our time” – has promised to “speed up a just ecological transition, boost renewable energy, move towards greater energy autonomy, and turn sustainability into a source of employment, innovation and prosperity”. The conservative People’s party (PP) has vowed to “act from science and without dogmatism” when it comes to fighting climate change and pursuing decarbonisation. Meanwhile the far-right Vox party, which could well form a coalition with the PP, has pledged to tackle “climate fanaticism” and to put an end to international agreements that “hinder our productive development and the prosperity of Spanish workers, families, businesses and industries”. View image in fullscreen Destruction in the province of Valencia, where hundreds of people died in flash floods in 2024. Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The Guardian Even though Spain’s three biggest parties enthusiastically defend their very different climate policies on paper, some observers are unsurprised at their reluctance to place them centre-stage at rallies and in interviews. Jordi Muñoz, an associate professor of political science at the University of Barcelona, is part of a team that has researched the effect that natural disasters, such as the Valencia floods, have on voter behaviour. “Our research reveals that the 2024 floods significantly increased the perception among Valencians that their region is particularly affected by climate change,” he said. “However … this did not translate into greater concern about climate change relative to other issues, nor did it increase the likelihood of people identifying climate change as one of the country’s top three problems. “Furthermore, we observed no increase in support for climate policies, nor any rise in individual actions taken to mitigate climate change.” Given the lack of votes to be had on the issue, Muñoz added, it’s hardly unexpected that parties opt to “pay it no attention during the campaign”. Nuria Blázquez, a spokesperson for Ecologists in Action, acknowledges that the sheer scale and effects of the climate crisis are a tough sell. Even after the fires, floods, heatwaves and droughts of recent years, both politicians and voters tend to focus on specific failings in disaster response rather than the over-arching cause. “In the case of the Valencia floods, the discussion was centred on whether the proper alerts were sent,” she said. “With the wildfires, the focus shifts to a lack of vegetation clearing or similar factors – problems that are somewhat easier to address. “Climate change feels a bit more abstract; it’s clearly a problem, but it’s so difficult to tackle that the general public finds it much easier to look for a culprit in simpler, more tangible things.” But Blázquez also warned that a huge amount is at stake as Spain prepares to vote – and that the results of the election will be felt well beyond the country’s borders. Under the leadership of the prime minister Pedro Sánchez – and his former environment minister Teresa Ribera, who now serves as the EU’s green transition chief – Spain has become what she terms the bloc’s “leader in environmental and climate policy”. But Sunday’s election could change all that. “Neither the PP – and especially not Vox – seem to acknowledge the reality of the situation. In fact, Vox’s narrative suggests that climate change basically doesn’t exist,” added Blázquez. “So we have no reason to be hopeful about a potential PP-Vox government … Without a doubt, that’s where the biggest loss would be: the total disappearance of any hope for leadership on environmental and climate issues within the EU.” Explore more on these topics Spain Climate crisis Extreme weather Europe Pedro Sánchez features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness
